item.research_question: What are the plastic deformation mechanisms at the micro/nanoscale of graphene oxide-reinforced high-entropy alloy composites, and how do they differ from pure HEA?
item.material_system: Fe22Co24Cr20Ni23Al11 HEA matrix reinforced with 0.0, 0.3, 0.6, and 1.0 wt.% Graphene Oxide (GO)
item.processing_route: Spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 900°C for 5 min under 45 MPa pressure and 10 Pa vacuum; micropillars (3 μm diameter, aspect ratio 2) fabricated via FIB with [001] orientation; MD simulations using LAMMPS with 1 fs time step and 12 m/s compression rate.
item.test_conditions: Micropillar compression to 0.30 strain at 2 × 10−3 s−1 strain rate; MD nanopillar compression (12 nm diameter) under NVT ensemble at 300 K.
key_findings: Hardness increased with GO content up to 0.6 wt.% (7.09 GPa for A3) then decreased to 6.31 GPa for 1.0 wt.% (A4).
Yield strength and flow stress of composites were higher than pure HEA, peaking at 0.6 wt.% GO.
Pure HEA micropillars showed localized deformation with single slip traces, while 0.6 wt.% GO composites exhibited homogeneous deformation.
MD simulations revealed only mobile 1/2 <111> perfect dislocations in pure HEA, whereas composites contained immobile <100> interstitial dislocations.
GO sheets effectively impeded dislocation movement, causing dislocation congestion above the sheet in composites.
Composites with 1.0 wt.% GO showed reduced strengthening due to GO sheet aggregation and Cr carbide segregation at grain boundaries.
The yield strength of composites climbed and then declined with increasing GO content, with the maximum at 0.6 wt.%.
item.mechanism: Strengthening is attributed to grain refinement (pinning effect of GO sheets) and the formation of immobile <100> interstitial dislocations via reaction of 1/2 <111> perfect dislocations on {110} planes. These immobile dislocations pin mobile dislocations and restrict their motion, requiring higher stress to activate deformation sources. Additionally, GO sheets physically block dislocation propagation, limiting plastic deformation to the upper region of the nanopillar.
item.limitations: The text states that the essential cause of the reduced strengthening efficiency in the 1.0 wt.% sample was initially unrevealed, though later attributed to agglomeration and segregation. It also notes that the HEA sample used has a substantial BCC structure which results in weaker plastic deformation compared to FCC structures, potentially limiting the observation of stress bursts.
quotes: The immobile <100> interstitial dislocations also participated in the plastic deformation of composites, in contrast to pure HEA counterpart where only mobile 1/2 <111> perfect dislocations dominated deformation.

The mechanical properties of HEA/1.0 wt.% GO composite showed a slight reduction compared with HEA/0.6 wt.% GO composite. This correlated with the compositional segregation of Cr carbide and aggregation of GO sheets.
